notes: Interim suspension extension application; Crane J refused adjournment and granted 12-month extension with summary costs assessment.

enrichment.short_title: GMC v Amarasingha: 12-month extension of interim suspension
key_facts: Dr Amarasingha faced serious GMC allegations including requesting a loan from a patient's carer and removing patient files, which he had admitted.
An Interim Orders Committee suspension from February 2003 was due to expire and only the court could extend it.
The doctor had prior findings of serious professional misconduct in 1990 and 1994 before restoration in 1997.
He did not attend and solicitors sought an adjournment for representation, which Crane J refused given the imminent expiry and history of non-attendance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by the GMC for a 12-month extension of an interim suspension order.
enrichment.outcome: Extension of interim suspension for 12 months granted; GMC costs summarily assessed at £3,000 rather than the claimed £4,500.
enrichment.ratio: Where serious admitted misconduct persists, prior IOC concluded no conditions could protect the public, and a substantive hearing remained uncertain, a full 12-month extension of interim suspension was justified despite protracted proceedings partly caused by the doctor's adjournment requests.
legal_issues: Whether to adjourn the extension application to allow legal representation
Whether a shorter extension than 12 months was appropriate
Whether GMC costs of the extension application should be awarded and at what level

confidence.notes: Short ex tempore judgment with clear outcome on extension and costs.

notes: Landmark VAT composite supply appeal; Court of Appeal allowed appeal finding separate zero-rated supply of course materials.

enrichment.short_title: College of Estate Management: VAT on distance-learning course materials
key_facts: The College provided distance-learning professional courses with bespoke printed binders produced at Reading, not sold separately on the open market.
Customs treated the supply as a single exempt education service, denying input tax recovery of about £60,000 per annum.
Students paid one fee and spent about 94% of study time on the printed materials with minimal face-to-face teaching.
The VAT tribunal and Lightman J held there was one principal exempt supply of education with printed matter ancillary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Lightman J dismissing the College's appeal against a VAT tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to the tribunal to apportion the price between exempt educational services and zero-rated books.
enrichment.ratio: Where printed course materials are physically and economically dissociable, constitute a substantial part of the consideration, and are an aim in themselves for distance-learning students, there are distinct supplies: an exempt education service and a zero-rated supply of books, not a single composite supply.
legal_issues: Whether printed materials were ancillary to a single supply of education or a separate supply of goods
Application of Card Protection Plan and related VAT single-supply authorities
Whether zero-rating of books trumped exemption for closely related goods
linked_authorities: Card Protection Plan Ltd v Customs & Excise Commissioners (C-349/96) [1999] 2 AC 601
Customs & Excise Commissioners v FDR Ltd [2000] STC 672
Customs & Excise Commissioners v British Telecommunications plc [1999] 1 WLR 1376

confidence.notes: Detailed reasoning on VAT supply characterisation with clear appellate disposition.

notes: Persistent hoax emergency-call offender; eight-year concurrent sentences upheld on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: R v Lowrie: appeal against sentences for hoax emergency calls
key_facts: Robin Lowrie, aged 24, had made hoax calls to emergency services since childhood, with repeated convictions and failed supervision, probation and custodial sentences.
After a five-year sentence for public nuisance he resumed hoax calls within two months of release.
In February 2004 he received concurrent eight-year sentences for 12 further public nuisance offences including false fire, ambulance and coastguard calls.
Psychiatric evidence diagnosed severe personality disorder with high risk of repetition and limited treatability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave of the single judge against concurrent eight-year imprisonment sentences.
enrichment.ratio: Despite psychiatric mitigation and a arguably high starting point, society is entitled to protection from persistent hoax calls that divert emergency services and risk fatal delay to genuine victims; long custodial sentences were warranted where all prior interventions had failed.
legal_issues: Whether the judge selected too high a starting point for concurrent eight-year terms
Relevance of personality disorder and failed treatment to sentence length
Protection of the public from repeat hoax emergency calls

confidence.notes: Facts, psychiatric context and dismissal are clearly recorded.

notes: Section 94 clearly unfounded certification upheld for Moldovan gay asylum claim; relocation to Chisinau evidence decisive.

enrichment.short_title: Bazdoaca: clearly unfounded certification of Moldovan gay asylum claim
key_facts: Cozmin Bazdoaca claimed asylum based on persecution as a gay man in Moldova, including street assaults in Balti after a former partner publicised his sexuality.
The Home Secretary certified the claim as clearly unfounded under section 94(2), relying on internal relocation to Chisinau.
Country evidence showed discrimination and isolated violence but an emerging gay scene, police protection at Pride events, and legislative reform pressure linked to EU accession.
The claimant's account in Balti was accepted as credible for present purposes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a section 94(2) clearly unfounded certificate in an asylum and Article 3 claim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; certification upheld as justified on the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: General intolerance and isolated assaults fall short of persecution or Article 3 ill-treatment; where objective evidence shows no real risk of systematic persecution in Chisinau and adequate state protection at Pride and elsewhere, no arguable case exists for an adjudicator and certification was lawful.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant faced a real risk of persecution or Article 3 breach if returned to Moldova
Whether internal relocation to Chisinau was reasonably available
Lawfulness of certifying the claim as clearly unfounded under section 94(2)
linked_authorities: L v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] 1 WLR 1230
Bagdanavicius v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 1 WLR 1207

confidence.notes: Detailed country evidence analysis and clear refusal of relief.

notes: Case management judgment allocating multiple Dow Jones/Al Rajhi libel appeals across two hearing slots.

enrichment.short_title: Al Rajhi and Dow Jones libel appeals: case management directions
key_facts: Multiple related libel actions involved Al Rajhi Banking Corporation, Dow Jones and Wall Street Journal Europe publications.
Sedley LJ granted renewed permission to appeal on international banking norms in one action and adjourned a presumption-of-falsity point to the full court.
Outstanding appeals raised Reynolds privilege, Bonnick v Morris, presumption of damage, burden of proof of falsity, and disclosure issues.
Parties cooperated on tabulated proposals for dividing issues between two three-day hearing slots.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management hearing for permission to appeal and listing of a coordinated group of libel appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted in 2004/1105; other permission applications disposed of or adjourned; appeals listed in two tranches with skeleton directions and possible further hearing for residual Dow Jones issues.
enrichment.ratio: Related libel appeals raising common Reynolds, privilege and presumption issues should be managed by grouping shared questions of law in the first hearing slot and reserving remaining issues, including presumption of falsity where no plea of justification exists, to a second slot or further date if necessary.
legal_issues: Whether permission to appeal should be granted on international banking norms
Whether presumption of falsity should be heard where no plea of justification was pleaded
How to allocate Reynolds privilege, Bonnick, damage presumption and disclosure issues across hearings
linked_authorities: Reynolds v Times Newspapers Ltd [2001] 2 AC 127

confidence.notes: Procedural orders are explicit though substantive libel merits were not decided.

notes: Children Act placement dispute for disabled teenager; council's Insight placement preference not unlawful at hearing date.

enrichment.short_title: Twomey v Calderdale: judicial review of special residential placement choice

statutes_considered.title: Arrangements for Placement of Children (General) Regulations 1991

key_facts: Louise, nearly 18, had pathological demand avoidance syndrome, epilepsy and a long history of failed residential placements after leaving Focus Arc in January 2004.
Calderdale preferred Insight in Bury while Louise and her parents insisted on Hesley College; expert evidence favoured Insight for developmental needs.
Louise firmly refused Insight and threatened absconding; Calderdale considered her biddable with structured support.
Proceedings began in November 2002 and had been repeatedly adjourned seeking compromise.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review, with leave, of Calderdale's refusal to place Louise at Hesley College and preference for Insight.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; Calderdale was not in breach of statutory duties at the date of hearing, but adjournment was ordered for early September if Louise remained unpersuadable.
enrichment.ratio: Section 20 requires due consideration of a 16-year-old's wishes but not automatic compliance; where Insight was the better placement on expert evidence and the authority's view that the child might accept a trial placement was not irrational, refusal to order Hesley was lawful though urgency required swift resolution if persuasion failed.
legal_issues: Whether Calderdale breached section 20 duties by refusing Hesley
Weight to be given to Louise's entrenched placement preference under section 20(6)
Whether it was reasonably practicable to secure agreement to an Insight trial placement

confidence.notes: Fact background is extensive and the interim disposition at the August 2004 hearing is clearly stated.

notes: Assault damages appeal; Court held injured feelings should be general not aggravated damages and reduced award to £4,500.

enrichment.short_title: Richardson v Howie: aggravated damages in bottle assault appeal
key_facts: Miss Richardson, a masseuse, was assaulted by Mr Howie with a broken bottle during a Barbados holiday argument, causing permanent scalp and thumb scarring.
The judge awarded £10,000 including £5,000 aggravated damages but gave no reasons for the aggravated element.
Mr Howie was later convicted of soliciting her murder and sentenced to six years.
The Court of Appeal reassessed scarring within JSB less significant scarring bracket (£2,000–£7,250).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against quantum and the award of aggravated damages after delayed written reasons.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; award reduced to £4,500 general damages covering scarring and injured feelings; aggravated damages set aside.
enrichment.ratio: In assault claims compensation for indignity, distress, humiliation and anger arising from the circumstances of the attack should normally be awarded as ordinary general damages, not as aggravated damages except in wholly exceptional cases; here £10,000 was excessive.
legal_issues: Whether injury to feelings in an assault should be compensated as aggravated or general damages
Appropriate quantum for permanent scarring and emotional injury
Effect of inadequate reasons for aggravated damages under English v Emery Reimbold
linked_authorities: A.B v South West Water Services Ltd [1993] QB 533

confidence.notes: Appellate restatement of aggravated damages law and substituted award are explicit.

notes: Long-running anonymised care proceedings; Munby J criticised EPO process and recorded withdrawal of care applications after rehabilitation.

enrichment.short_title: X Council v B: care proceedings, EPO process and withdrawal after rehabilitation
key_facts: Care proceedings concerned three brothers removed under emergency protection orders in January 2003 after long social services involvement and allegations of exaggerated or fabricated symptoms.
Parents denied threshold facts but eventually consented to withdrawal of care applications after children were rehabilitated home under interim arrangements.
Munby J recorded traumatic impact of summary removal, heavy-handed contact supervision, and gaps in EPO appeal rights potentially engaging Article 8.
On 13 May 2004 he granted leave to withdraw applications for care orders in respect of two children while recording parties' disputed positions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court public law care proceedings including case management, rehabilitation planning and final withdrawal of care applications.
enrichment.outcome: Care applications withdrawn by consent on recorded terms; proceedings ended without a contested threshold determination; judgment also addressed procedural deficiencies in EPO removal and contact supervision.
enrichment.ratio: Emergency removal and continued care proceedings must be proportionate and handled sensitively; where rehabilitation succeeded and no order was now necessary the court should disengage, but the statutory EPO scheme requires anxious scrutiny of Convention rights given limited review and appeal mechanisms.
legal_issues: Proportionality of emergency removal and interim care orders under Article 8
Whether EPO statutory limitations on appeal and discharge comply with human rights standards
Appropriate use of interim care orders to manage rehabilitation
Local authority contact supervision practices
linked_authorities: Re B (Care: Interference with Family Life) [2003] EWCA Civ 786

confidence.notes: Very long judgment but final withdrawal order and EPO/human rights analysis are clearly articulated.

notes: Family committal appeal; Wall LJ dismissed challenge to suspended committal for breach of non-molestation undertakings.

enrichment.short_title: De Montford v McKenzie: appeal against suspended committal for undertaking breaches
key_facts: Mr McKenzie gave undertakings not to harass Mrs De Montford, not to write or telephone her, and not to enter within 400 yards of Greenfield House except on the highway.

Wilson J found breaches including parking near the property, a 10-mile slow-driving harassment incident, an anonymous letter in the letterbox, and letters to a hotel vendor calculated to obstruct her purchase.
He imposed suspended 28-day committal orders and additional injunctions.
Mr McKenzie appealed as a litigant in person chiefly on alleged defects in the notice to show cause under CCR Order 29.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against suspended committal orders made by Wilson J sitting as an additional judge of Rhyl County Court.
enrichment.ratio: Order 29 requires a fair notice of alleged breaches but need not be perfect where the judge refined allegations and the respondent was not prejudiced; findings of breach based on documentary evidence and credible witness testimony warranted suspended committal even if some procedural complaints were made.
legal_issues: Whether committal proceedings should have been dismissed for defective notice to show cause
Whether Wilson J was entitled to proceed without further adjournment
Whether findings of breach of undertakings were supported by evidence
Propriety of relying on a judge's earlier credibility assessments

confidence.notes: Findings, penalties and procedural rulings are comprehensively explained.

notes: Community care JR for autistic young adult; flawed fettering on placement choice is clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Alloway v Bromley: community care placement unlawfully ruled out on cost

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Stephen Alloway, a profoundly autistic 19-year-old with severe learning difficulties and epilepsy, needed a suitable 52-week placement after leaving Purbeck View School.
His parents wanted Hesley Village & College in Yorkshire; Bromley offered Robinia Care or Solent Residential Homes instead.
A section 47 assessment by Mark Smith recommended Hesley at about £3,725 per week, but the council ruled Hesley out from at least February 2004 as unnecessarily expensive.
The council's July 2004 offer of Robinia and/or Solent was quashed because Hesley had been excluded without a fair, informed comparison of suitability and costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Bromley's decision refusing placement at Hesley Village and offering alternative residential placements.
enrichment.outcome: The council's placement decisions were quashed for unlawfully fettering discretion and flawed decision-making; the court declined to order placement at Hesley but granted costs and liberty to apply on urgency.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority may consider resources when choosing between suitable placements, but it acts unlawfully if it rules out a potentially suitable option on cost before viable alternatives are properly assessed and without an accurate like-for-like comparison.
legal_issues: Whether Bromley breached its section 47 duty to assess and decide on community care services
Whether the authority unlawfully fettered its discretion by excluding Hesley on cost grounds
Whether Robinia or Solent were suitable placements meeting Stephen's assessed needs
Whether the court should substitute its own placement decision
linked_authorities: R v Gloucestershire County Council, ex parte Barry [1997] AC 584
R v East Sussex County Council, ex parte Tandy [1998] AC 714
R (S) v Leicestershire County Council [2004] EWHC 533 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on fettering and quashing orders are explicit; merits of alternative placements were not finally determined.
